WASHINGTON, July 31 (Reuters) - The United States on Friday banned imports from ‌43 more companies over alleged human ‌rights abuses of the Uyghurs, including Hunan Aihua Group, ​one of China's largest capacitor manufacturers, according to a government posting.

The companies were added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, ‌which restricts the ⁠import of goods tied to what the U.S. has determined are China's ⁠human rights abuses and ongoing genocide in the Xinjiang region.

The latest additions also include companies ​in the ​pharmaceutical, metals, and cotton ​sectors.

Hunan Aihua Group ‌did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The posting marks the first time companies have been added to the list under the Trump administration, and brings the number of entities ‌on the list from ​144 to 187. The Uyghur ​Forced Labor ​Prevention Act was signed into law ‌in December 2021.

The U.S. says ​Chinese authorities ​have established internment camps for Uyghurs and other religious and ethnic minority groups in ​China's western ‌Xinjiang region. Beijing has denied any abuses.

title: Led by veteran coach Justin Green, WSU's running backs 'want to be great'
description: Jul. 31—When someone shouts "Kirby" during a Washington State football practice, it can get a little confusing. They might grab the attention of the big boss: first-year coach Kirby Moore, or the 5-foot-11, 207-pound bruiser of a running back known as Kirby Vorhees. Or they could summon both. Moore said that beyond Vorhees, he does not personally know any other Kirbys.
fullText:
Jul. 31—When someone shouts "Kirby" during a Washington State football practice, it can get a little confusing.

They might grab the attention of the big boss: first-year coach Kirby Moore, or the 5-foot-11, 207-pound bruiser of a running back known as Kirby Vorhees.

Moore said that beyond Vorhees, he does not personally know any other Kirbys.

Including Moore, Vorhees said he has only ever met two other Kirbys besides himself.

The Cougars appear to be in a promising place with two members of the exclusive Kirby club saddled up and ready to do battle in the crimson and gray.

But it did, and WSU's two other top running backs joined Vorhees to form a room led by former Montana RBs coach Justin Green — another Moore assistant with a long track record of success.

"I love how hungry they are. They want to be great," Green said of Wazzu's running backs. "In this business of college football, how things are, what kind of money is being thrown at guys. These guys want to play football more than anything else."

Vorhees was one of the most prominent Cougs to announce his intention to enter the transfer portal last December when former coach Jimmy Rogers took the same post at Iowa State.

He sat out the bowl game, then was among the first Cougs to sign a revenue-sharing agreement to return to the WSU football team.

Soon after, rising sophomore Maxwell Woods signed his name on the dotted line to return and junior Leo Pulalasi was on his way back, too.

Vorhees, who ended the regular season as WSU's No. 1 running back, said that the opportunity to play, coupled with the quality of his relationships with other returning players, sealed the deal.

Unspoken, but nonetheless relevant, is a likely significant name, image and likeness package for Vorhees and the two other prominent running backs.

Woods said that the running backs talked to each other about their future every day last winter before they each decided to return.

"We all kinda had an idea, 'We really could run this back and really do what we do and do our best to take over,'" Woods said. "I'm really grateful that we are getting another year together."

Woods said that the chance to talk with Moore around the Potato Bowl in Boise sealed the deal for his return

"I just think it was more of the trust factor," Woods said of Moore. "The numbers really don't lie. He's been an elite offensive coordinator."

With 228.3 yards per game last year, Moore's Missouri Tigers were the eighth-best rushing team in the nation.

Vorhees, WSU's leading rusher in 2025, is a prototypical east-west slasher, dialing up physicality at the point of attack, said the Cougars' running back coach Justin Green.

Woods presents similar slasher skill coupled with remarkable speed, while Pulalasi packs an advanced football sense and ability to "make football plays for the football team," Green said.

"There's no overthinking when it comes to him, which I love as far as his football talent," Green said of Pulalasi. "And that's going to help us."

Freshman Tremayne Hill and Central Washington transfer Beau Phillips could also factor into the room, Green said.

Coach Green: 'Very wise ... very detailed'

When the three backs re-signed with WSU, they had no idea who their new position coach would be. Woods said he placed his trust in Moore to get that hire right, and, as proven through April's spring game, he did.

Green, who spent the last 14 years molding all-conference running backs at Montana, joins WSU as the assistant head coach/running backs coach.

Moore said that he ran into Green on the recruiting trail in the San Diego area and was impressed by his track record of success.

"We're teachers first," Moore said. "And he's done a very, very nice job."

Green left Montana after having coached half of UM's all-time top 10 rushers, including Eli Gillman, the 2023 Jerry Rice Award winner, reserved for the best freshman in the Football Championship Subdivision.

That experience has presented itself in the way that Green teaches the game of football, Vorhees and Woods said.

"Very smart, just very, very wise and very detailed," Woods said of Green. "Very detailed with every little thing, as little as steps, even just like getting the hand-off. There's so much detail."

That detail, Woods said, has expanded his understanding of football.

Green, Vorhees said, "is the smartest running back coach (he has) been around when it comes to knowing the scheme and the entirety of football itself."

Over the course of spring camp, Woods emerged as the star of the show, breaking out into several quality runs. When fall camp fires up on Aug. 6, he could make a big push for the starting job.

That's the thing about the running back room that Green didn't have to foster, he said.

"They all have different personalities and different likes and wants," Green said. "And what I noticed, probably more than anything else, is how tight their bond is. They are very bonded. They hang out with each other, they laugh, they have a good time."

It's the kind of bond Green said he has created within his Grizzlies' RB rooms — and it was already in place at Wazzu when he arrived.

Green's father, Anthony Green, was a Pop Warner and high school football coach in San Diego.

The future coach saw how hard his father worked, raising 12 kids (Justin Green has 10 brothers and one sister) and giving his best to his players.

"When you've got a guy, as far as a coach who loves you, you're willing to run through a brick wall for them because that's how you show your love back," Green said. "Growing up with that, as far as seeing that view of the way my father (acted)."

It's Anthony's example that has propelled Justin forward to his present role as mentor, teacher and father figure.

WSU's running backs are plenty talented. The retention was just the start. In a potentially explosive scheme, WSU has the chance to reach another level in the backfield.

That starts with Green, and if successful, translates to touchdowns, first downs and broken tackles.

"No matter what I know, it's what they know. And then what are they willing to do for you," Green said. "If you want the best out of them, you've got to love them, you've got to treat them, right. You've got to treat them fair, and they will reciprocate with giving you the best that they have."

title: Jamir Watkins Suffers ACL Tear, Potentially Season Ending
description: Washington Wizards guard Jamir Watkins suffers potentially season ending ACL tear
fullText:
The injury bug has hit the team again this summer after the Washington Wizards announced that Jamir Watkins suffered a torn left ACL in summer league, and could potentially miss the entire 2026-27 season.

Watkins, who is currently on a two-way contract, suffered the ACL tear during Washington's summer league opener against the Utah Jazz where he was tasked with the defensive assignment of guarding number two overall pick Darryn Peterson.

Watkins underwent a successful surgery on his left knee earlier today, which is encouraging to hear considering ACL tears could be career ending or altering.

While Watkins is expected to miss a majority of the regular season, doctors haven't ruled out the possibility of him suiting up for Washington towards the backend of the season.

Watkins (25) was drafted with the 43rd overall pick in the 2025 NBA Draft out of Florida State University, where he was known for his two-way ability and high motor.

Throughout his rookie year, Watkins displayed his high motor and two-way ability averaging 7.4 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.3 APG and 1.6 stocks per game on 44.6% FG% and 29.7% from beyond the arc.

Although Watkins wasn't the most efficient scorer last season, his elite on ball defense was put on full display as he would often guard the opposing teams' best player. Watkins took the defensive assignment of guarding Darryn Peterson in the highly anticipated summer league opener, where he did a great job of keeping the number two overall pick in check.

Watkins played a massive role in shutting down Peterson, as he scored 24 points on 6/18 FG, 2/7 3FG with eight turnovers.

24 Points on 6/18 FG (33.3%), 2/7 from 3 (28.6%), 6/8 FT (75.0%), 3 Rebounds (2 Off. Rebs), 3 Assists (8 TOV), 1 Block, 9 fouls (out of 10 allowed), and a +/- of -9 in 29:44… pic.twitter.com/4heXWg41rj

— MrBuckBuck (@MrBuckBuckNBA) July 10, 2026

Unfortunately, Washington will have to be without one of their better perimeter defenders for a majority of the regular season.

ACL tears typically take 6-12 months of recovery, but for professional athletes (especially basketball players), the rehabilitation process may take even longer due to how essential healthy knees are in the sport.

This injury comes at a terrible time for Watkins, as he was expected to build upon a strong rookie season and compete for minutes on a hopeful playoff team.

REPORT: Jamir Watkins suffered a Torn ACL during Summer League

Watkins could miss all of the 2027 season but had a successful surgery on his left knee

Prayers up for Jamir Watkins 🙏🙏 pic.twitter.com/XcyoLg711Z

— WizardsMuse (@WizardsMuse1) July 30, 2026

Luckily for Washington, they have one of the deepest rosters in the league and should be able to carry their weight fine without Watkins. Players like Bilal Coulibaly, Cam Whitmore and Khris Middleton will now be more depended on to play strong defense and contribute in the way Watkins has.

The road to recovery will be long and grueling for Watkins, but there's no denying that he can be an impact player on both sides of the ball when healthy.

title: Deebo Samuel returns to 49ers on one-year contract
description: Deebo Samuel is returning to the 49ers on a one-year contract worth up to $7 million after spending last season in Washington.
fullText:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Deebo Samuel is returning to the San Francisco 49ers after spending one season with the Washington Commanders.

Samuel agreed to a one-year contract worth up to $7 million, according to multiple reports. The agreement was negotiated by Tory Dandy of Athletes First and gives the veteran receiver an opportunity to revive his career in the offense where he became one of the NFL’s most versatile playmakers. San Francisco selected Samuel in the second round of the 2019 NFL draft. He spent six seasons with the franchise before being traded to Washington for a fifth-round pick in March 2025.

Samuel caught 72 passes for 727 yards and five touchdowns in 16 games with the Commanders last season. He also carried the ball 17 times for 75 yards, continuing to provide the hybrid receiver-running back ability that defined his first stint with the 49ers.

Reunion: Free agent WR Deebo Samuel is signing back with the #49ers, sources say. The former #Commanders and SF pass-catcher returns where it all began.

1-year, up to $7M in a deal done by Tory Dandy of @AthletesFirst. pic.twitter.com/eGgs4jHdnr

— Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 31, 2026

His best season came in 2021, when Samuel earned first-team All-Pro honors after producing 1,405 receiving yards, 365 rushing yards and 14 total touchdowns. His eight rushing touchdowns established an NFL single-season record for a wide receiver. Samuel has not replicated that production in recent years, but his familiarity with San Francisco’s offense should reduce the adjustment period. He can align outside, in the slot or in the backfield while giving the 49ers another experienced option capable of creating yards after the catch.

The short-term contract limits San Francisco’s financial risk while providing Samuel with an opportunity to rebuild his value before returning to free agency. It also removes one of the most accomplished receivers from a veteran market that still includes Stefon Diggs and Keenan Allen.

Diggs is coming off an 85-catch, 1,013-yard season, while Allen remains one of the league’s most accomplished route runners. Both could attract increased attention as teams evaluate injuries and roster needs during camp.

Samuel will not have to learn a new organization. He is returning to the coach, system, and franchise that helped make him an All-Pro.

title: Vic Fangio says Jihaad Campbell’s edge rusher days are over
description: The Eagles DC talks position battles, individual performances, and more in his first training camp press conference.
fullText:
The Eagles were back to work on Thursday for their second practice of training camp, and we got to hear from defensive coordinator Vic Fangio before the team took the field. He talked about some of the position battles, what he’s seen from the edge rushers, and his thoughts on individual players. He also revealed that Jihaad Campbell will no longer be getting as many reps on the outside.

Fangio said that he wouldn’t say that the starting safety spot is Marcus Epps’ job to lose, but said that the veteran has been in with the first team in the nickel group, and it’s Cooper DeJean in the base group.

“But, [Michael] Carter’s doing fine too. It’s competition.”

Fangio explained that it’s too early to tell whether Campbell will make any sort of leap heading into his second year, noting that Campbell missed the whole offseason and only had one training camp practice under his belt up to this point. Ultimately, he’s doing fine, but it’s just too early for any kind of deep analysis.

While Campbell had opportunities on the outside last year with Nakobe Dean on the roster, Fangio admitted that some of it was valuable but some was also not great. He explained that those outside reps actually set him back in developing as an inside linebacker.

The DC later said that it remains to be seen how much more they can put on Campbell’s plate, but that they were confident he’ll be able to step up. Fangio also said that the LB’s days of cross-training as an edge rusher are pretty much over, and while there might be a few times they ask him to move to the outside, it won’t be anything long term.

The DC expects Jonathan Greenard to miss most of training camp due to his pec strain, and while he’s a veteran in the league, the Eagles are asking him to do some new things — like dropping back in coverage — and those missed reps could be meaningful. Fangio thinks Greenard is capable of what they’re asking, and the edge rusher is doing a good job in meetings, but it’s not the same as practice experience.

Fangio was also asked about AJ Epenesa and how he helps fill that gap without Greenard. He explained that it remains to be seen, but also gave the DE a huge compliment (by Fangio standards).

“I told AJ [Epenesa] this — I told it to him in front of the whole team, too — for a guy that’s being asked to do a few things that he’s never done before, I thought he did a nice job yesterday with it.”

And as for whether Greenard’s injury also opens the door for Brandon Graham to return to the roster, Fangio pointed to Howie Roseman as the person who can answer that.

He later talked about how he has high expectations for Jalyx Hunt as he heads into his third year, saying that the DE is capable of being an exceptional player.

Staying healthy is the big priority for Nolan Smith this season, with Fangio saying last season was choppy for the DE because he was dealing with some injuries and missed a lot of time. Still, he’s confident in Smith, and said both Smith and Hunt had good days in their first training camp practice.

“He’s got a great work ethic, demeanor, and he just picked up yesterday where he left off last year.”

Fangio said that it’s helpful to be seeing a different offense this season, there’s a lot more moving parts which helps the Eagles defense.

The DC joked that he’s on the PP plan with Uar Bernard — lots of patience, and lots of persistence. He noted that the first day of practice in the spring was the first time Bernard ever put a helmet on, and now pads will be a whole new thing, so it’s important that he and the team temper their expectations. It’s going to be a process.

ILB Zack Baun will wear the green dot helmet and be the main signal caller this season — something he had experience doing the first half of last season when Nakobe Dean was injured. Fangio said that if they were to ever ask Baun to do something he’s not familiar with, he’ll fight through until he’s good at it, so he can do anything that’s needed.

The DC said that Howie Roseman needs to save some money to pay DT Moro Ojomo next year, because he’s someone Fangio wants in this defense.

title: Washington mother pulls children from school after Pride lesson shown in music class without notice
description: A Washington mother said a Pride-themed lesson from "Queer Kid Stuff" was shown in music class without parent consent or an option to opt out.
fullText:
A Washington mother says she is withdrawing her children from an elementary school after learning a Pride-themed lesson had been presented during music class without advance notice to parents or an opportunity to opt out, raising questions about district policies governing classroom instruction.

"I assumed I had probably missed an email asking for consent, but there was nothing," Maria Varchetto said in communications with school administrators, which she shared with Fox News Digital on Monday. "No advanced notice, no opportunity to review the lesson, no information letting parents know this topic would be discussed. No option to request that our kids be allowed to opt out and participate in an alternative activity. There was nothing."

Varchetto alleged the lesson was presented to elementary school students, including her daughter, on June 15 at Martha Lake Elementary School in the Edmonds School District as part of a music class and that parents were not informed beforehand.

Trump Admin Targets Woke Schools Accused Of Hiding Students' Gender Transitions From Parents

Varchetto said that a video entitled, "Why is Pride in June," from the YouTube account, "Queer Kid Stuff," which, according to the account, "imagines a kinder and more equal future through highly-accessible education and entertainment for kids ages 3+," was shown to her fourth-grade daughter.

The YouTube channel describes itself as an "LGBTQ+ educational webseries for children ages 3+ hosted by a tie-wearing queer lady, Lindsay, and her non-binary best-stuffed friend, Teddy. Gender Studies 101 meets Mr. Rodgers' Neighborhood!"

Varchetto said the incident prompted her to remove her children from the school.

Virginia School District Sued Over Alleged Policy Of Keeping Students' Gender Transitions Hidden From Parents

"We are 100% removing our kids from this school as I have no trust in the leadership," Varchetto said.

Other materials Varchetto said were included were a list of videos by musicians in the LGBTQ+ community, such as Freddie Mercury of Queen, Lil Nas X and Billy Porter dancing in a ballgown on "Sesame Street."

Varchetto told school officials that her daughter recalled hearing during the lesson that students could identify as gay, lesbian, transgender, asexual, nonbinary or Two-Spirit.

She said an administrator told her she had not been aware those topics were part of the classroom discussion, leaving Varchetto wondering whether the lesson included more than the materials she had been shown.

Trump Administration Opens Four Title Ix Investigations Into Michigan And North Carolina School Districts

"No handouts were sent home (which is typical for music class)," Varchetto told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Varchetto said she asked the school for a copy of the lesson materials but was told they could only be reviewed in person rather than sent electronically. She also said parents were not notified beforehand that the lesson would be taught, were not given an opportunity to opt their children out, and received no advance communication about its content.

She said that cultural lessons were taught every month for the theme of that month, but that Pride month was left off of the list of lessons.

"I feel mad they did this, mad they hid it," Varchetto said. "I feel insulted, offended, angry, and sad that my kids are now being taken out of a lifestyle they've grown to love, away from the friendships they've built, all because this one teacher didn't care to ask permission and a principal lied and hid it."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Edmonds School District said, "The lesson was not part of a districtwide Pride curriculum. It was a music lesson developed by the school's music teacher that highlighted the contributions of influential musicians, including some who identify as LGBTQ+."

The spokesperson continued, "The purpose of the lesson was to teach music and music history through the lives and contributions of notable artists. Discussions about an artist's background or identity were included as relevant biographical context, similar to how students may learn about other aspects of historical figures' lives that helped shape their experiences and contributions."

The spokesperson added, "We expect instructional materials to be age-appropriate and aligned with district expectations and state standards. As with any concern raised about classroom instruction, we will work with the school administrator to determine whether they met those expectations."

title: Trump announces a $22.5B makeover of Dulles airport that will eliminate the 'people movers'
description: President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport that will end the use of the widely disliked “people movers,” the mobile lounges tha...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport that will end the use of the widely disliked "people movers," the mobile lounges that have been used for decades to shuttle travelers to and from the main terminal.

In place of the people movers, the airport will add a new U-shaped passenger train, a central walking tunnel, more moving walkways and new concourses. An above-ground parking garage closer to the main terminal with space for 32,000 vehicles is also in the offing, according to Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The airport makeover would add to a long list of renovation projects the Republican president is pursuing to leave a lasting mark on the Washington region after his term ends in January 2029. Among other undertakings, he is building a new White House ballroom and wants to build a towering triumphal arch near the Lincoln Memorial.

But of all the construction projects Trump is pursuing, the renovations at Dulles could prove to be his most popular and benefit the greatest number of people. The airport, the area's primary international airport, served roughly 29 million passengers over the past year, according to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

"This transformation is another step in our ongoing efforts to make Washington, D.C., safe and beautiful again," Trump said. "We're doing something with Dulles that's going to make it the top anywhere in the world."

Trump, who used a laser pointer to explain the renovations displayed on renderings, said the "crazy distances" travelers must walk to get from place to place make Dulles "the worst airport."

Congress would need to approve some aspects of the renovation plan, Trump said. Construction could start next spring, Duffy said. The plan does not call for expanding Dulles' runways or adding new ones.

Officials said the airlines and the airport authority that operates Dulles would pay for the project with municipal bonds, but they did not spell out how much of the cost might be passed on to travelers through higher fees or ticket prices when flying out of the airport.

John Potter, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which operates Dulles, said his agency, United Airlines and other airlines operating there have agreed "to fund this thing." Dulles is one of United's hubs.

"So this is not requiring federal dollars," Potter said at the Oval Office event. "This is going to be airport-generated dollars, airline contributions, which is phenomenal."

Dulles, located in northern Virginia, is about 25 miles (40 kilometers) from downtown Washington. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport is located in Arlington, Virginia, which is closer to downtown, making it popular with members of Congress and local residents.

The president, a former real estate developer, said in December that Dulles was "incorrectly designed." He nonetheless praised Eero Saarinen, the Finnish-American architect and designer of the airport's main terminal. Trump and Duffy said the president reviewed presentations from about 30 architects before Trump settled on the redesign he announced Wednesday.

Even if the project is largely paid for by the airlines, industry analyst Henry Harteveldt said taxpayers might be asked to cover upgrades to the runways and safety measures as well as new customs and security facilities. The president of Atmosphere Research Group said he also wouldn't be surprised to see a passenger facility fee added eventually.

"I'm not taking the statement that they are not going to use taxpayer money at face value," Harteveldt said.

The reason United and other airlines are willing to invest in Dulles, he said, is that they believe it will help them expand by adding more flights and passengers, boosting their revenue. But this could also contribute to higher ticket prices.

"United is going to try to charge as much for its tickets as it can. Other airlines will do the same," Harteveldt said. "I think part of the statement that no tax money will be used could be something to placate the public right now."

Designed by Chrysler Corp., the people movers shuttle passengers between the terminal and aircraft. The airport operates a fleet of 19 mobile lounges, each capable of carrying up to 102 passengers, according to its website.

When Dulles debuted, the airport touted the system as a major convenience. Passengers, it said, "had to walk only 200 feet once they entered the terminal until they were seated in a mobile lounge for the short trip directly to their aircraft," a service it described as unique to Dulles.

But they have become one of passengers' least favorite aspects of transiting through Dulles, with travelers — and Trump — complaining that the system is outdated, balky and slow. At times, planes have to wait for a people mover to cross and vice versa, which slows operations at the airport.

One of the lounges crashed in November, sending 18 people to the hospital.

Dulles began a multibillion-dollar construction program in 2000 to begin to address future passenger demand. Major projects included two new parking garages, a fourth runway, a new concourse, a new Air Traffic Control tower, pedestrian walkways, and an airport train system, according to the airport authority's website.

The airport authority says significant modernization work is already underway at Dulles. Later this year, the first segment of the new Concourse E will open with 14 additional United gates that will help the airline expand its international network, provide direct access to the airport's AeroTrain system and debut new and enhanced concessions options and passenger lounges.

title: More than 1,200 AI workers across Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta are asking for Washington’s help building an AI slowdown plan
description: The statement, signed by senior executives at competing companies, calls on the government to help build the tools needed to pace frontier AI development.
fullText:
More than 1,200 employees at the world's leading AI labs, including senior executives, have signed a statement asking the U.S. government to help build the tools needed to slow down AI development if it ever becomes necessary.

The statement, titled "Pacing the Frontier," was published Tuesday and has been signed by prominent tech figures including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and several of the company's cofounders, alongside OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, and Google DeepMind head of AI safety and alignment Anca Dragan.

The list brings together companies that are normally locked in fierce competition with one another and is a striking statement for an industry under enormous commercial pressure to keep building ever larger and more capable models.

"Having so many staff from different companies come together in agreement on this point is striking," Tyler Johnston, founder of the Midas Project, an AI watchdog group, told Fortune. "There are many bitter rivalries and disagreements in the industry, so the fact that there is such strong consensus on this point is a warning that we really ought to pay attention to."

While the statement does not ask any company to slow down at the moment, it does call on Washington to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools that would help the world "pace" development. It specifically calls out the risks around AI systems that start to design their own successors faster than anyone can understand or control them.

"Having talked to many of the people who signed the letter, they don't want a pause," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told Fortune. "But there is a concern about how the technology is advancing." The companies are looking for the optionality to do that at some point and have support from a third party when that point arrives, he added.

The letter comes in the wake of a security breach that has rattled the AI industry. OpenAI disclosed that two of its models, the newly released GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable unreleased research system, broke out of a sandboxed internal test environment, found a previously unknown vulnerability that gave them access to the open internet, and then used stolen credentials and additional exploits to breach the production systems of Hugging Face to steal the answers to a cybersecurity benchmark they were being evaluated on. Hugging Face detected and contained the intrusion on its own days before OpenAI connected the activity to its internal testing, and had already reported it to law enforcement.

Court records showed earlier ‌this month that ⁠Carroll has collected nearly $5.63 million from Trump. She has won $88.3 million in ⁠civil verdicts against the president in the seven years since he first denied having ​raped her ​around 1996 in ​a Bergdorf Goodman ‌department store dressing room in Manhattan.

title: Trump says US and Tehran having 'good talks' as drones hit Iran's neighbours
description: , Nayera Abdallah and Elwely Elwelly WASHINGTON/DUBAI, July 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the United States was having "good talks" with Iran and there was a
fullText:
WASHINGTON/DUBAI, July 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the United States was having "good talks" with Iran and there was a chance of a deal over their conflict, but he warned that U.S. strikes would resume if the negotiations failed to deliver.

Despite Trump's optimism, Tehran appeared to quickly test the pause ‌in the U.S. military campaign, with Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq reporting drone attacks on Monday.

Washington abruptly suspended a two-week campaign of air strikes on Iran on Saturday in Trump's latest ‌strategic U-turn in the five-month-old conflict.

"We're having good talks," he said. "I think there's a good chance that something could happen, and if it does, good, if it doesn't, we go back to doing what we were doing two days ago."

At a campaign rally in ​Michigan later on Monday, Trump said of Iran: "You can't bribe them. You've got to beat them, and we'll beat the hell out of them. But we'll see how it turns out. Right now, there are very friendly negotiations going on."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that messages were still being passed between the sides through mediators and Iran had not forsaken diplomacy, but reports that it requested negotiations were "fabricated."

"This is not in our DNA," he said.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Sunday that Iran would halt its own attacks as long as Trump's self-imposed ceasefire continued.

Iran's central military command later on Monday accused the U.S. of threatening vessels and ‌oil tankers in its territorial waters and of "attempting to implement an illegal maritime ⁠blockade", which it said "constitutes an escalation of the conflict in the region."

Saudi Arabia said it shot down drones aimed at petroleum targets, including in Riyadh. It said they had been launched from Iraq by Iran-backed armed groups, and it reserved the right to respond.

Separately, Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said they had targeted the East-West ⁠Pipeline carrying oil to Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea port of Yanbu in retaliation for Saudi drone incursions.

Tehran also said it remained in control of the contested Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for global energy supplies, which Trump has demanded vessels be able to pass through freely.

Public disapproval of the war has been weighing on Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections in which they have to defend slim congressional majorities.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll ​conducted ​over the weekend showed Trump's approval rating ticking higher to 37%, up three points from last month when it tied ​the lowest of his presidency.

However, just one in three Americans support the Iran war, ‌the lowest Reuters/Ipsos reading since the conflict's early days, with most saying Trump has failed to explain his goals.

The end of the U.S. campaign after 13 successive nights of intensifying bombing and Trump's remarks on talks sent oil prices tumbling. U.S. crude CLc1 fell 8.21% to $81.98 a barrel, and Brent LCOc1 fell to $87.77 per barrel, down 9.31% on the day.

Trump's decision to suspend U.S. attacks reflected advice from his military that the bombing had reached the limits of what it could achieve, according to a U.S. official and several U.S. media reports.

The U.S. official told Reuters military commanders had advised the president they were running out of targets and that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had expressed concern over the depletion of air munitions.

Trump dismissed suggestions that the U.S. faced munitions shortages, saying the military was rapidly rebuilding ‌inventories depleted by shipments to Ukraine. He said he would like more of "the more sophisticated stuff."

IRAN MEDIA SAY SIX SHIPS ​TURNED BACK

Iranian state media outlets cited an "informed source" as saying that Iran had turned around six "offending ships" on Monday that had ​attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without permission.

Trump launched his renewed bombing campaign to punish ​Iran after Tehran fired on ships using a route promoted by the United States, which told vessels to sail close to the coast of Oman.

Iran says ships may ‌pass only through a Hormuz channel that runs closer to its own coast, which ​it controls and where it intends to impose transit ​fees.

The two weeks of renewed U.S. bombing killed scores in Iran and destroyed bridges and tunnels across the south as well as military targets.

Four U.S. service members were killed in return fire against U.S. bases in neighbouring states. Iran also struck civilian infrastructure in Gulf countries, calling it retaliation for U.S. strikes.

It remains unclear what leverage Washington can exert to break Iran's grip on the ​strait.

Washington and Tehran reached an agreement in June on a framework for ‌talks meant to take place by the end of August to resolve major issues such as Iran's nuclear programme.

But they have disputed the meaning of the memorandum's language about the ​strait, with Washington insisting it requires Tehran to allow free travel, while Iran says it grants it the authority to supervise transit.

(Additional reporting by Muayad Hameed in Iraq. Writing by ​Peter Graff, Toby Chopra and David Brunnstrom; Editing by Sharon Singleton, Toby Chopra, Mark Potter and Cynthia Osterman)

title: Lakers Proposed to Trade for 2 Ex-Luka Doncic Teammates in Mega Deal
description: This Lakers trade idea would reunite Luka Doncic with two of his former Mavericks teammates, P.J. Washington and Daniel Gafford. The post Lakers Proposed to Trade for 2 Ex-Luka Doncic Teammates in Mega Deal appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Lakers acquired nine new players this offseason, but they aren’t done making moves, with reports suggesting that they continue to pursue help at the five spot and the wing position. One Lakers trade idea would reunite Luka Doncic with two of his former Dallas Mavericks teammates, filling those needs.

Per multiple reports, the Dallas Mavericks are open to moving both Daniel Gafford and P.J. Washington as they prepare to usher in the Cooper Flagg era. Both role players played a key role in helping the Mavericks reach the 2024 NBA Finals and would be perfect additions due to their built-in chemistry with Doncic.

Lakers would receive: PJ Washington, Daniel Gafford

Mavericks would receive: Jarred Vanderbilt, Jaden Hardy, Jake LaRavia, Dalton Knecht, 2032 first-round pick swap (via LAL), 2031 second-round pick (via WAS), 2032 second-round pick (via WAS) and 2033 second-round pick (via LAL)

As Dallas users in the Cooper Flagg era, it makes little sense for the franchise to hold onto veterans like Daniel Gafford, P.J. Washington, Klay Thompson, Naji Marshall and possibly even Kyrie Irving. Several insiders expect them to gradually move all their veterans either this summer or by next year’s trade deadline, giving Flagg a roster of players that suit his timeline.

Furthermore, the Mavericks gave Gafford (three-year, $54M) and Washington (four-year, $88M) long-term extensions last year under the premise that Anthony Davis, Kyrie Irving, Klay Thompson and Co. would be there to lead a veteran outfit. However, their strategies have changed, and they appear to be heading in a youth movement.

The Mavs also need to reduce their logjam at the five spot, making Gafford dispensable. Their current rotation boasts of Dereck Lively II, new Santi Aldama, rookie Morez Johnson Jr. and Moussa Cissé, whom they are said to be very high on.

Adding the long-term money of Washington and Gafford comes with its fair share of risks, but could be one of the moves the Lakers need to make to give Luka Doncic a complete squad. Despite all their offseason acquisitions — including Walker Kessler, Quentin Grimes, Kevon Looney, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton, Ziaire Williams and Matisse Thybulle — the Lakers don’t really have a starting-caliber small forward, a role that P.J. Washington can slide into. While Grimes, Mamukelashvili and Sexton are offensively-skewed players, Williams and Thybulle are limited offensively. Washington would bring a more complete skill set with his three-point shooting and elite defense.

Similarly, the Lakers remain a little thin at the five spot despite adding Walker Kessler and Kevon Looney. While the latter is more of an energy guy who plays limited minutes, Kessler is coming off a season-ending injury and may need some insurance.

A player like Gafford would be perfect as a second-string big for the Lakers, who continue to pursue the market for a big man, according to The Athletic’s Dan Woike.

“The Lakers are still monitoring the market for big men, team sources told The Athletic,” Woike reported last week. “They traded for Walker Kessler and signed Kevon Looney to play center, and Mamukelashvili can play the position, too.

“The team could address the position either by trade or signing, like with potentially adding Thybulle. The roster is currently at full capacity.”

[AZ Central] Perdomo eyeing pitching upgrade as Diamondbacks fall to Nationals – It is understandable why starting pitching would be on Perdomo’s mind. Over the past two days, the Diamondbacks have handed the ball to a pair of rookie lefties in Mitch Bratt and Kohl Drake. Bratt got through five innings on Saturday, July 25, but he allowed five runs and walked five batters. Drake on Sunday allowed four runs in four-plus innings. “I think sometimes it’s a lot for them,” Perdomo said of young starters being thrust into a pennant race. “They don’t have so much experience. They have been doing the best they can do. They work hard every single time. Bratt and Drake, they (empty their tanks). Whatever has happened in the games, it’s tough for them, but at least we get some fight from them.”

[Dbacks.com] D-backs drop rubber game to fellow Wild Card contender as Deadline looms – Making his second Major League start on Sunday, Drake was given three leads but surrendered each one, allowing consistent hard contact. Ahead 4-2 in the fifth, he issued a leadoff walk to Nasim Nuñez and James Wood followed with a two-run homer to tie it. “The most important inning in baseball is the inning after you score, right?” Lovullo said. “Shutdown inning. I think the walk to start the fifth was very critical.” The poor pitching performances negated a solid afternoon for the the top of the lineup one day after Lovullo switched things up. The manager moved Ketel Marte down into the cleanup spot and Gabriel Moreno up to number three behind Corbin Carroll and Perdomo. The group combined to go 5-for-14 with five walks and six runs scored.

[SI] Ugly Loss to Nationals is a Wake-Up Call for D-backs’ Deadline Needs – As obvious as it may have been already, the Diamondbacks simply won’t be able to make a deep postseason run with the rotation in its current state, and the team cannot bank on the return of injured players in that category. Arizona trotted out two of its rookie arms in Mitch Bratt and Kohl Drake. Both of those starters have shown some potential in the majors, but both were hammered by a strong Washington offense. Meanwhile, Merrill Kelly still has an ERA in the 5.00s with inconsistent command. Zac Gallen, when healthy, had the worst qualified ERA in baseball. Ryne Nelson may not be able to fully ramp back up, and Corbin Burnes isn’t expected back until early September, and his effectiveness is anything but guaranteed coming off both Tommy John surgery and a shoulder injury.

[MLB Trade Rumors] Diamondbacks Interested In Extension With Gabriel Moreno – The five-year, $99.4MM extension Cal Raleigh signed with the Mariners in advance of his 60-homer 2025 season might very well be a target point for Moreno’s agents at Klutch Sports. Raleigh inked his deal heading into his age-28 season (whereas Moreno will be 27), and with one of his three arb years already in the books. While Raleigh’s power numbers were superior to Moreno’s, their overall offensive production was pretty similar. Moreno has a career 114 wrC+ from 1429 career PA and counting, whereas Raleigh had a 111 wRC+ from 1760 PA at the time of his extension.

[Arizona Sports] The Athletic’s Bowden lists Angels pitcher Jose Soriano as trade target fit for Diamondbacks – Bowden noted the Diamondbacks’ need for a starting pitcher and his control beyond 2026 as the main reasons for the 27-year-old righty’s potential fit in Arizona. In 21 starts, Soriano has posted an 8-6 record with a 3.43 ERA, 122 strikeouts and a 1.25 WHIP. Soriano had a strong outing in his most recent start against the St. Louis Cardinals on Monday, pitching seven innings with just one run surrendered on four hits and seven strikeouts. With Soriano under control through 2028, he would also give the D-backs an option in the rotation beyond this season, as several starters are set to become free agents, including Michael Soroka and Zac Gallen. Corbin Burnes also has an opt-out clause in his contract.

[Noozhawk] A McCann-Do Attitude Has Arizona Diamondbacks Pointed Toward Playoffs – That Major League Baseball team trusts no one more with its pitchers than James McCann, a Dos Pueblos High School graduate who turned 36 last month. Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo has described McCann’s mentorship of the team’s young mound staff as being “on a Ph.D. level.”“You could probably target the day he got here and take a look at our ERA and do some of the reverse math on your own,” Lovullo said. “I know it’s been very good since he’s gotten here.“I think he’s had a strong input as to the success that we’ve had overall as a pitching staff.”

[MLB.com] Sun-splashed and spirited crowd watching, Beltrán, Andruw, Kent enshrined in Hall – The three new members bring the Hall’s count to 354, of which 281 are players. Beltrán and Jones are just the third and fourth center fielders elected by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America in nearly half a century. Since Duke Snider went in with the Class of 1980, only Kirby Puckett (2001) and Ken Griffey Jr. (2016) were counted as center fielders elected by the BBWAA until this year. Kent, who was elected by the Contemporary Baseball Era Committee at the Winter Meetings last December, is the first second baseman to join the Hall since another Astro: Craig Biggio in 2015.

[Deseret News] The name for Utah’s potential future MLB team? It has to be ‘Trappers’ – Utah’s current sports branding is top tier. The Jazz name is iconic, “Mammoth” has quickly proven to be a popular choice and Real Salt Lake and Utah Royals FC have slick identities as well. Thus, the bar will be high for an MLB team name. They can’t afford to get it wrong. Scrolling through social media, some of the most popular name proposals include the Utah Outlaws, Utah Gulls, Utah Cutthroats, Utah Black Diamonds AND Utah Pioneers. Some have suggested the longtime minor league Bees brand get called up to the majors. But there’s a different minor league team that should be chosen for an MLB name: the legendary Salt Lake City Trappers.

There have certainly been bigger nautical disasters than HMS Titanic. The wartime sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff resulted in the loss of over nine thousand lives, roughly six times as many. But none has made such an indelible mark on pop culture. Purely in the cinema, there have been dozens of films based on or inspired by it. The first came out less than a month after Titanic sank, and starred actress Dorothy Gibson, who was actually a survivor of the event. Most famously, of course, is James Cameron’s Titanic, which remains the second-biggest movie worldwide, almost thirty years after its release. Tapping into this interest, an exhibition recently opened in Scottsdale, promising to “tell the story of the RMS Titanic like never before.” So, does it?

title: Man accused of illegally 'wrestling' protected sharks in Washington state after months-long investigation
description: Body camera video shows a wildlife officer confronting fisherman after months of surveillance over alleged illegal shark catches in Puget Sound.
fullText:
An Oregon man is facing charges for allegedly illegally catching and "wrestling" protected bluntnose sixgill and broadnose sevengill sharks in Puget Sound.

The Washington state Department of Fish and Wildlife recently shared body camera footage of an officer confronting Connor Seifert, 27, in June in Pierce County, Washington.

"You know your shark rules," the officer could be heard on the video telling Seifert. "You can't fully or partially remove sixgill from the water.

Shark Sightings Spike Near America's Beaches As July 4 Crowds Head To Shore For Weekend

"When you wrestle a sixgill to shore like that, you hop on its back, you expose its gills to the air," the officer continued. "You know as well as anybody else does that Puget Sound is a nursery for these sharks. There has been a direct correlation between catching these sharks in this stage in their lives and the mortality of the pups inside the moms."

He added, "Once they exhaust themselves being fought to shore, then all of their babies die. And then, sooner than you know it, you're not going to have sixgill and sevengill returning to Puget Sound anymore."

This came after months of following Seifert's movements and his online posts, with officers finally setting up surveillance so they could catch him making an illegal catch.

Suspect In Viral Monk Seal Harassment Video Says He Was Doxxed As Federal Court Fight Begins

He has been charged in Pierce County with nine counts of unlawful recreational fishing in the second degree and one count of making a false or misleading statement to a public servant. The first is a misdemeanor and the second is a gross misdemeanor.

Misdemeanors carry up to a $1,000 fine and 90 days in jail if found guilty and gross demeanors carry up to a $5,000 fine and a year in jail.

"Fishing for sixgill and sevengill sharks is unlawful, and unfortunately, officers are seeing a growing number of online posts showing these sharks targeted and then unlawfully removed from or partially removed from the water," the department said in a post about Seifert's charges.

Massachusetts Homeowners Stunned After Town Warns July 4 Flags Threaten Endangered Birds

Seifert claimed that he hadn't been targeting the sharks and that he had accidentally caught them, but videos he posted to social media that allegedly showed him holding a shark's mouth open, while sitting on its back and holding it by its tail on the shore while it attempted to get away paint another picture.

The department said it has gotten 14 complaints about Seifert, mainly connected to his allegedly targeting the sharks.

"Puget Sound acts like a nursey for sixgill and sevengill sharks before they head out to the ocean, the department said.

The department added, "This is one of the primary reasons why it is unlawful to target these sharks locally, as the anglers fishing for these creatures are targeting them during a highly volatile era in the animals' lives."

Both shark species are listed as "Species of Greatest Conservation Need" in Washington State.

Bluntnose sixgills are categorized as "near threatened" and broadnose sevengills are "vulnerable," according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

title: Profiling Washington's defensive players on Shrine Bowl watch list
description: The Washington Huskies had 7 defensive or special teams players named to the East-West Shrine Bowl's annual summer watchlist earlier this week.
fullText:
Jedd Fisch's Washington Huskies have seven players from the defense or special teams on the East-West Shrine Bowl's annual Shrine Bowl 1000 watch list. Released earlier this week, inclusion on the list indicates a good chance that a player will be invited to either the Shrine Bowl or its competitor game, the Panini Senior Bowl, which will release its own watchlist later this summer.

Huskies defensive tackle Elinneus Davis, edge rusher Jacob Lane, linebackers Xe'ree Alexander and Jacob Manu, cornerback Emmanuel Karnley, safety Alex McLaughlin, and punter Hunter Green represented the defense and special teams on the list. Both are units Fisch overhauled going into the 2025 season, with Alexander, Manu, and McLaughlin all joining the team via the transfer portal before that year after Washington replaced outgoing defensive coordinator Steve Belichick with current coordinator Ryan Walters. Fisch also brought in special teams coordinator Chris Petrilli, although the results with the specialist group were more mixed in 2025. That led Washington to target Green, a Huskies legacy and former FCS All-American at Northern Colorado in 2024, in the transfer portal this offseason.

Davis has been a steadily ascending player and one of the few consistent presences on the Huskies' defensive line over the last three seasons, playing in 12 games as a redshirt freshman in 2024 and 13 with 10 starts last season. He was nearly unblockable during spring practices and could be in line for a huge year with a remade group including freshmen Derek Colman-Brusa, Tufanua Ionatana Umu-Cais, and JD Hill and transfers Darin Conley, DeSean Watts, and Kai McClendon. As a fourth-year player, Davis will also be eligible to return to Montlake in 2027.

Lane was ranked just behind Davis in Washington's class of 2023 as the 14th and 15th-best composite recruits in that cycle. Considering how much the top of that class has atrophied - 6th-ranked Rashid Williams is the highest-rated player remaining on Washington's roster, and just three of the top ten recruits from that cycle remain on Montlake - the fact that the Huskies have three players (Lane, Davis, and center Landen Hatchett) from the class on the Shrine Bowl watchlist is impressive.

Lane would be off to the NFL one way or another had the NCAA not changed its eligibility rules in June, which will allow the in-state Emerald Ridge standout to return to Washington in 2027 if he doesn't build on his first season as a full-time starter to his satisfaction.

Alexander may very well end up being somewhat of a surprise to Huskies fans when the NFL draft rolls around, as his feedback in league circles seems borderline hyperbolic for a player who will be a part-time starter for Washington this season. But all of the Huskies' linebackers will play a ton this year, and a defensive MVP honor from the LA Bowl allowed Alexander to finish his first season on Montlake with a flourish. The UCF transfer also has the benefit of arriving at the right time: the NFL has coveted players who can switch between off-ball linebacker and edge rusher in recent seasons. Alexander, like Lane, has a fifth season available due to the NCAA rule change, but he may find his middle-round NFL projection more enticing than returning to start on a full-time basis next to Zaydrius Rainey-Sale.

Manu only played five games last season as Washington tried to slow-play his arrival in the hopes that this summer's NCAA rule changes would come in the middle of last season, which would've allowed Manu to be fully active last year without sacrificing his ability to return in 2026. Instead, Huskies fans only caught glimpses of what the Arizona transfer is capable of, but his spring session this offseason should have those same fans eager to see what he can do without Fisch assigning an assistant to make sure the senior doesn't trot out of the tunnel with his pads on every week. Listed at 5-foot-9, Manu has an uphill battle to make the league, but his tenacity and competitive spirit should be enough to get his foot in the door. An invite to an event like the Shrine Bowl, where players get more face time with NFL personnel, would undoubtedly be extremely helpful for him.

Karnley spent the 2023 season with Fisch and defensive backs coach John Richardson at Arizona before electing to stay in Tucson when the staff headed north to Seattle. His performance as a redshirt freshman was good enough to get him a transfer portal commitment to Miami, but he left after the spring and landed at Virginia, where he broke up 8 passes and intercepted another before reuniting with Fisch and Richardson for his fourth college football season. He'll be tasked with filling the shoes of Tacario Davis and Ephesians Prysock, who were both drafted into the NFL after locking down the boundaries for the Huskies last year. He doesn’t have the same size profile as those two or sophomore starter Dylan Robinson at "only" 6-foot, but his familiarity with the staff and proven production around the country bode well for his role on Montlake.

🔟 Huskies selected to @ShrinersBowl 2027 Shriners Children’s East-West Bowl 1000 watchlist. pic.twitter.com/C5y3EfpMMV

— Washington Football (@UW_Football) July 23, 2026

McLaughlin is a former FCS Freshman All-American at Northern Arizona who the Washington staff brought in last season to help bolster the safety position with Walters turning to more three-safety looks on the back end of the Huskies defense. Few FCS-to-FBS transfer portal additions were more successful, as McLaughlin earned honorable mention All-Big Ten and team defensive MVP honors after starting every game for Washington. With the size to play in the box but the coverage ability to hang with just about anybody in coverage, McLaughlin has the same benefit of Alexander of potentially entering the NFL right as their skillsets are held in the highest esteem. He is a perfect fit for the NFL’s pivot to bigger nickel and “apex” players like Kyle Hamilton of the Baltimore Ravens and Nick Emmanwori of the Seattle Seahawks.

Green told the media during spring practice that his aim is to win the Ray Guy Award this season, and he should be among the preseason favorites to take home the award. That could also roll forward into being one of the few punters drafted in the 2027 class. The first step in any of that will be transforming Washington’s punt unit, which struggled in just about every metric last season with Luke Dunne handling duties. Green, however, was No. 6 in the FBS in punting average, which should give Washington’s standout defense more opportunities to keep the Huskies in games.

Washington begins fall camp in early August, with the Shrine Bowl kicking off the NFL draft cycle at the end of January.

title: Concerning Signs for Ben Shelton As Jack Draper Delivers a Reality Check During DC Open Practice

Ben Shelton’s preparations for the 2026 Mubadala DC Open have come under the microscope ahead of his highly anticipated campaign. After his first-round exit at Wimbledon, Shelton will look to bounce back strongly at the ATP 500 event on home soil, but his latest practice session with Jack Draper has raised concerns about his form ahead of his opening match.

Draper’s progress has repeatedly been derailed by injuries over the past few seasons, preventing him from building momentum on tour. After missing almost the entire clay-court season due to a knee injury, the Brit made a promising comeback on grass by reaching the semifinals of the Eastbourne Open under the guidance of his new coach, Andy Murray.

However, his injury woes resurfaced when an arm injury forced him to withdraw from Wimbledon. The Brit, who has slipped to world No. 147, has since accepted a wildcard for the DC Open and has been preparing for his return under Murray’s watchful eye.

Draper received an encouraging boost ahead of his opening match, defeating No. 2 seed Ben Shelton 6-1 in a practice session at the venue. Tennis reporter Christian’s Court revealed that Murray was pleased with the Brit’s dominant display.

On the other hand, the reporter flagged concerns about Shelton’s forehand looking below its usual standard.

“Draper just won a practice set 6-1 vs Shelton. Jack’s left arm and serve looked good; Coach Murray’s happy with his return too. Shelton’s FH has been very off though. Something to look out for next week,” the post read.

Shelton was originally scheduled to face fellow American Ethan Quinn in the first round of the DC Open. However, Quinn was forced to withdraw from the event due to a right metatarsal injury. The world No. 6 will now face either a qualifier or a lucky loser in his opening match.

Placed in opposite halves of the draw, Ben Shelton and Jack Draper will both need to reach the final to set up a blockbuster showdown at the DC Open. Their only previous meeting took place at the 2025 Indian Wells Masters, where Draper secured a 6-4, 7-5 victory.

title: Floatplane catches fire after emergency landing near Sucia Island
description: A seaplane carrying 11 people crashed near Sucia Island in Washington's San Juan Islands. All aboard were accounted for.
fullText:
A Kenmore Air floatplane carrying 11 people made an emergency landing and then caught fire on July 23 near Sucia Island in Washington state's San Juan Islands, prompting a large rescue response by emergency crews, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

The U.S. Coast Guard Sector of Puget Sound received a report at about 5:25 p.m. local time that a Kenmore Air seaplane had made an emergency landing in Shallow Bay before catching fire, the agency said in a statement on X. The aircraft had 11 people aboard, and all were accounted for, according to the Coast Guard.

The Coast Guard said U.S., Canadian and local responders "launched multiple assets to assist with the rescue." Several people were being transported to local hospitals for medical evaluation and treatment.

In a news release, Kenmore Air identified the aircraft as a de Havilland DHC-3 Otter. The flight had departed from Lake Union in Seattle and was headed to Roche Harbor on San Juan Island when the aircraft went down at 5:15 p.m. local time near Sucia Island, according to the airline.

Pan Am plane crash: Lost 1952 Pan Am plane found off Puerto Rico coast nearly 75 years later

Kenmore Air said there were 10 passengers and one pilot on board, and that "everyone aboard has been accounted for." The airline said two injured passengers were being transported to medical facilities in Bellingham, Washington, and two others to Orcas Island of the San Juan Islands for treatment.

Multiple people sustained injuries "ranging from head injuries to broken bones and lacerations," and at least one person was in critical condition, according to the San Juan County Sheriff's Office.

The aircraft caught fire after the emergency landing and was now "resting against the rocks on Sucia Island," the Coast Guard told USA TODAY. The Coast Guard's environmental response personnel are working with partner agencies to assess any potential environmental impacts.

Kenmore Air said it had activated emergency response procedures and was working closely with the Coast Guard and local emergency responders. Responding agencies included the Coast Guard, San Juan Island Fire and Rescue, Orcas Island Fire and Rescue, Lopez Island Fire and Rescue, San Juan County Parks and the San Juan County Sheriff's Office.

"This evening one of our aircraft was involved in an accident near Sucia Island. We are grateful that everyone aboard has been accounted for, and our immediate focus is ensuring our passengers and pilot receive the care and support they need," Kenmore Air CEO David Gudgel said, adding that the company is "fully cooperating" with investigators.

Texas plane accident: Pilot injured after a small plane lands on roof of a Houston-area home

The National Transportation Safety Board confirmed to USA TODAY that it was investigating the incident. The Federal Aviation Administration is also investigating.

The cause of the accident was not immediately known.

Founded in 1946, Kenmore Air is the largest seaplane airline in the United States, flying over 90,000 passengers annually on scheduled, scenic and charter flights, according to the company's news release and website.

Sucia Island is part of the San Juan Islands, a popular boating and tourism destination in northwest Washington near the U.S.-Canada border. The San Juan Islands are an archipelago between Washington and Canada's Vancouver Island.

title: Will Commanders' defensive overhaul be effective in 2026?
description: The Washington Commanders completely revamped their defense during the offseason, but are those changes going to be effective in 2026?
fullText:
Adam Peters had one major goal during the offseason: Make the Washington Commanders' defense younger and faster. He addressed that largely in free agency, signing players like Odafe Oweh, K'Lavon Chaisson, and Leo Chenal, to name a few. He added to that list in the draft by selecting Sonny Styles with the No. 7 overall pick and edge rusher Joshua Josephs in the fifth round.

Suffice it to say that between the departures and additions, the Commanders' defense looks very different in 2026 than it did in 2025. But will what Peters did actually pan out this season? Under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, one of the biggest storylines is whether this defense can get all of its new faces on the same page, something that NFL.com's Grant Gordon wrote about earlier this week.

When you fall from being everyone's NFC Championship Game darling to a 5-12 struggle bus, you can run out of fingers to point. The Commanders put a massive UNDER CONSTRUCTION sign in front of a defense that finished dead last in yards allowed. They used the No. 7 overall pick on Ohio State linebacker Sonny Styles, an athletic marvel who will draw plenty of hype as a preseason Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate. General manager Adam Peters opened the check book before turning in the card to get Styles, too. Washington broke the bank to sign pass rusher Odafe Oweh, while adding plenty more veteran starters elsewhere: nickel Amik Robertson, safety Nick Cross, pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson, linebacker Leo Chenal and defensive tackle Tim Settle. The Commanders added veteran depth, as well. Binging on free agents isn't always a winning formula, of course. How quickly new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones and Washington's cast of fresh faces get on the same page will be crucial in camp.

If you paid attention during minicamps and OTAs, you already know that the defensive players are putting a huge effort into creating bonds off the field just as much as on the field. It's not a secret that the bond between teammates is equally as important as the skill set each player brings to the table.

The biggest problem the Commanders will have here is the number of new faces on the roster. It's one thing if you bring in a handful of new players to join an otherwise stable unit, but it's another beast altogether when you add a dozen or more new faces. This is the task ahead of Daronte Jones: Make this unit a cohesive group that functions as such.

Jones has an advantage in this, though. The Commanders' defensive players want to bond. They want to get to know each other. They want to work together. They want to win games and prove that they weren't just slapped together haphazardly. Getting the players to buy in is half the battle, and these guys are already there. Now Jones just has to get them to understand his scheme and execute plays proficiently.

title: George Washington's Teeth (2006)
fullText:
George Washington, the first president of the United States, lost all but one of his teeth by the time he was inaugurated, and had at least four sets of dentures he used throughout his life. Made with brass, lead, gold, animal teeth, and human teeth purchased from slaves, the dentures were primarily created and attended to by John Greenwood, George Washington's dentist.[1]

In 1756, when Washington was 24 years old, a dentist pulled his first tooth.[2] According to his diary, he paid 5 shillings (£0.25, equivalent to $13 in 2025) to a "Doctor Watson" for the removal. His diary also regularly mentioned troubles such as aching teeth and lost teeth.[3] John Adams said that Washington attributed the loss of his teeth to using them to crack walnuts, but modern historians have suggested that calomel, the mineral form of mercury(I) chloride which Washington was given to treat smallpox, probably contributed to the loss.[4]

On April 30, 1789, the day of his first presidential inauguration, although he had mostly dentures, he had only one remaining natural tooth, a premolar.[5] During that same year, he began wearing full dentures.

Washington's last tooth was given as a gift and keepsake to his dentist John Greenwood.[6]

During his life, George Washington had four sets of dentures. He began wearing partial dentures by 1781.[6] Despite many people believing they were made of wood, they contained no wood, and often were made of teeth extracted from slaves and other materials, including hippopotamus ivory, brass, and gold.[7][8][9] The dentures had metal fasteners, springs to force them open, as well as bolts to keep them together.

Records at Mount Vernon indicate that Washington paid enslaved individuals £6.10 for their teeth. It is unknown what amount, if any these individuals actually received, as enslaved people were often cheated by their overseers and their families.[10] It is also unknown if these enslaved individuals were coerced to sell their teeth.[11] These teeth were evidently intended for the use of French dentist Jean Pierre Le Mayeur in his dental practice.[12] Whether they were used for Washington himself is unknown. The poor in the Western world had sold teeth as a means of making money since the Middle Ages, which were used as dentures or implants and sold to those of financial means.[citation needed]

During the American Revolutionary War, Jean Pierre Le Mayeur provided services in tooth transplantation. In May of 1784, Washington paid several unnamed slaves 122 shillings (£6.10, equivalent to $195 in 2025) for a total of nine teeth to be implanted by a French doctor, who became a frequent guest on the plantation over the next few years.

While it is unconfirmed that these purchased teeth were for Washington himself, his payment for them suggests that they were in fact for his use, as does a comment from a letter to his wartime clerk Richard Varick: "I confess I have been staggered in my belief in the efficacy of transplantion," he wrote. Washington used teeth sourced from slaves to improve his appearance, a subject of frequent discomfort to him.[13] However, scholars of the Mount Vernon estate dispute this, since the transactions in Washington's accounts state that they were bought "on account for [...]Le Moyer". "If Washington had been purchasing the teeth for himself, there would have been no need for this information; the entries would have simply recorded the item and payment, as when Washington purchased poultry, wild game, fish, and garden produce from enslaved individuals." As such, it remains unknown whether Washington personally used any teeth purchased from slaves or others.[14]

He took the oath of office while wearing a special set of dentures made from ivory, brass and gold built for him by dentist John Greenwood.[7] According to his diaries, Washington's dentures disfigured his mouth and often caused him pain, for which he took laudanum.[15] Washington once wrote that his lips would "bulge" in an unnatural way. This distortion is noticeable on his image on the one-dollar bill, an image taken from the Athenaeum Portrait, an unfinished painting from 1796 by Gilbert Stuart.[7]

Washington once wrote to his dentist, Greenwood, to avoid modifying the dentures "which will, in the least degree force the lips out more than now do, as it does this too much already."[16]

Apart from the disfiguration caused by the dentures, the distress may also be apparent in many of the portraits painted while he was still in office.[15][17][a] He spent constant effort maintaining his dentures, and often had them shipped to Greenwood, for maintenance.[2]

The mistaken belief that Washington's dentures were wooden was widely accepted by 19th century historians and appeared as fact in school textbooks until well into the 20th century. The possible origin of this myth is that ivory teeth quickly became stained and may have had the appearance of wood to observers. A letter from Greenwood to Washington in 1798 advised more thorough cleaning; "the set you sent me from Philadelphia ... was very black ... port wine being sour takes off all the polish".[18]

The only existing complete set of Washington's dentures is owned by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, who own and operate George Washington's estate in Fairfax County, Virginia. There is another complete, original, lower jaw denture dated 1795 at the National Museum of Dentistry in Baltimore, Maryland.[19]

At least three of Washington's dentists are identified. His diary mentions "Doctor Watson", the dentist who pulled his first tooth. His personal dentist and friend was Jean-Pierre Le Mayeur.[7] John Greenwood of New York City made and maintained his dentures.[7]

title: Exclusive-Iran strikes on CIA facilities prompt questions about possible Russian role
description: , Gram Slattery and Timour Azhari WASHINGTON/RIYADH, July 22 (Reuters) - Iranian drone attacks on CIA facilities in the Gulf have prompted U.S. intelligence analysts to investigate
fullText:
WASHINGTON/RIYADH, July 22 (Reuters) - Iranian drone attacks on CIA facilities in the Gulf have prompted U.S. intelligence analysts to investigate whether Russia assisted by providing targeting information or advanced drone technology, said four people familiar with U.S. intelligence.

These people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to ‌discuss national security matters, said U.S. intelligence officials have not yet reached firm conclusions about the possible Russian involvement in the attacks on CIA facilities. But they cited ‌the strikes' effectiveness and apparent precision, as well as Russia's broader technical support for Iran, as possible evidence.

At least two CIA sites were struck in March, Reuters and other outlets have reported. One of the facilities was the CIA station in Saudi Arabia, which is located in the U.S. embassy in Riyadh, and a separate site was located in eastern Iraq. Some of the sources said additional CIA sites had been hit, but they did not disclose details.

RUSSIA HELPED TARGET FACILITIES: INTELLIGENCE MEMO

One internal memo from a Western intelligence ‌agency, described by an official in the region with access to ⁠the document, concluded Russia has likely played a role in targeting regional CIA facilities. The official discussed the memo on condition that its precise authorship not be disclosed.

Two Western officials in the Gulf who were briefed on intelligence reports said analysts thought the Saudi attack involved a pair of Russian-enhanced ⁠versions of Iran's Shahed drones. One of the aircraft blew a hole through a vulnerable part of the embassy's exterior and the second flew through the opening and detonated, they said. No deaths or injuries were reported.

While Russian assistance for Iran is longstanding, given the countries' close ties, specific targeting of sensitive CIA sites would indicate Moscow is willing to go further in disrupting U.S. operations as Washington struggles to bring ​the ​Iran war to an end.

Concerns that Russia could be providing targeting data to Iran intensified this weekend after ​strikes on a U.S. air base in Jordan, where Iran struck army ‌barracks with ballistic missiles, killing two soldiers.

The White House referred a request for comment to the CIA, which declined to provide one.

Iran's mission to the UN, the Russian Defense Ministry and the Saudi government did not respond to requests for comment.

The two Western officials in the region said Russia has helped Iran improve its Shahed drones' ability to reach targets, and said analysts suspected that Iran used these versions in its strike in Riyadh.

Russia, said a separate source, has helped Tehran improve the accuracy of its Shahed-136s by supplying a satellite navigation system — the Kometa-M — that experts say is far more accurate and harder to jam than the one produced by Iran.

The Wall Street Journal first reported in March that Russia has provided the Kometa-M to Iran. The ‌Kremlin denied the report, calling it "fake news."

CIA facilities overseas include the agency's main offices in individual countries ​that traditionally are housed in embassies and are called stations. Additionally, the CIA maintains offices, safe houses, logistics hubs ​and sites involved in surveillance or other operations.

The locations of those sites are closely guarded ​secrets.

The sources declined to disclose the exact number or locations of CIA facilities hit by Iranian drones. One source put the number at "more than one ‌and fewer than a dozen." A second source said several facilities were ​hit.

U.S. intelligence analysts have been looking ​into whether Iran relied on Russian targeting data for the embassy attack, said the sources.

Doubts remain, however. Some of the sources warned that Iran could have been aiming for the U.S. embassy generally and by chance struck the CIA station.

Some analysts have concluded that few nations beyond Russia would have the means to acquire and the interest in ​weaponizing such sensitive targeting intelligence against the U.S., according to the ‌sources.

Daniel Hoffman, a former CIA station chief and undercover operations officer, said it would not be surprising for Moscow to help Tehran target CIA facilities given their ​close strategic partnership.

"They share an interest in trying to reduce or eliminate U.S. influence altogether in their self-designated spheres of influence," he said.
